name: Hand drill
summary: A spindle spun between bare palms into a fireboard — the lowest rung of the ladder, needing nothing you did not grow or find.
time: 1-2 hours to make the set; 1-3 minutes of continuous work to run it

steps.text: Everything BONE DRY. A hand drill fails on damp wood before technique ever becomes the problem.
Cut a shallow socket near the edge of the fireboard, then a V-notch from the edge into about one eighth of it, cut all the way through.
Set the ember pan under the notch and pin the board with your foot.
Spin the spindle between flat palms, pressing DOWN as you run your hands from top to bottom of the spindle.
steps.why: Downward pressure is what makes heat; spin without it and you polish a glazed socket that will never take again.

steps.text: At the bottom of the stroke, snap your hands back to the top WITHOUT letting the spindle stop or lift.
steps.why: Every pause bleeds the heat you just made. The floating-hands hand-off is the whole skill.

steps.text: When black dust fills the notch and smoke rises on its own, stop and do not move the board.
Let the dust pile smoke by itself, then tip it into the tinder bundle and blow it to flame.

verify: Fine black powdery dust, not brown grit. Brown means too little downward pressure.
Smoke still rising 10-20 seconds after you have stopped is an ember.
limits: This is the hardest method here by a wide margin and the least forgiving of wet, cold, or tired hands. It is a skill to own before you need it, not one to learn in the situation.
It works reliably only with the right plant species for spindle and board, which is knowledge about YOUR ground that this record cannot supply.
cautions: Blisters end the attempt and then persist for days. Stop before the skin tears, not after.
A glazed, shiny socket has stopped generating dust — rough it up before continuing.
